has left will not be used to harmonize the
party, but rather through his relation to
men of prejudices to show evaporation in
the different parts of the country. What
else can be made of the beating of drums
for Holman, when Indiana has never asked
for Holman? It is merely another "on
to Richmond" noise and cannot be
attended with any respectable results. Mr.
Tilden has arrogated for several years past
the right either to get the nomination him-
self or to prescribe who should have it.
Like all concerted old men who have had
their day, he wants to have a hand in the
pie. It has been alleged that he was the
man who broke down Seymour and
Blaine in 1858 by influencing the New
York World to turn against them after the
October elections. In 1872 he kept
aloof from the Greeley move-
ment. Between that time and
1876 he seemed to be in a scheme to de-
stroy Chief Justice Church and Seymour
and get them out of the way. That is why
Kelly's bolt against Robinson had such a
powerful following in western New York,
where Chief Justice Church was regarded
as the typical Democratic statesman. In
1880 Mr. Tilden's relation to Hancock's
election was sufficiently mystical to have
been the subject within few months past
of exposures which have sigually shut up
the mouths of his chief fuglemen.
At the present time it would seem that
Tilden has just enough mentality left to
harass the younger men who are coming
into prominence.

Mr. Hewitt has just spoken of him in
downright terms as without gratitude or
propriety. I was told some months ago
by a gentleman who visited Greystone,
that when he mentioned Mr. Payne, of
Cleveland, as the proper person to nom-
inate next time, Tilden replied, "Oh,
Hoadley is a better man." Yet I hear
that when Hoadley has been
too much pressed in his presence he said
there is the greatest difference between
natural leadership and that kind of a
book craftsmanship which Mr. Tilden
possesses. The latter is very useful to
most of the country newspapers, and car-
ries away the college graduates.

went to see him, as I have been told, and

tenance with slight trace, I think, of high
living. Nevertheless he is a plain and

lowers, but incapable of putting up tricks

conceit, pulled up altogether beyond the

ination for the presidency the factions that

common sense and upright patriotism will

Plea for the MINORITY.

It is a surface axiom that the majority rules; as a matter of fact they do nothing of the sort. A minority rules always, and the multitude are led about like sheep by a few clever experts. But that state of affairs need not prevail in our Household, and I for one proceed to enter a plea for those of us who are only average.

Some of our members desire that a change be made, and our communications become strictly edifying, and we waited, that mere pleasantness, friendly discourse, and personal mention be ruled out, and elevation to a high literary standard be the aim of all writers. Now that is all very well, but wholly subversive of the idea of a Household. Those who are so anxious for literary development, and higher culture, forget the majority. The most of who read newspapers are people of average cultivation, and average talents. If literary excellence is insisted upon, then we, who are by far the largest number, are ruled out.

And again, while fine writing is always desirable, and never out of place, still the average newspaper reader is as much entertained as he desires to be by ordinary writers. For my own part I sometimes read absolute trash from deliberate choice. I am too tired to follow an author in higher lines of thought, and so I want to escape from myself. Households in newspapers must be like households in everyday life, and we all know that the geniuses in the average family are counted by only one in any.

Those who can write elegantly are at liberty; nay they owe it to themselves and their readers always to do their very best; but they must not shut the door in the faces of those of us who are not so highly endowed. The average writer will please the average reader, and the majority are average always!

Come along, then, with me, sisters, who belong to the vast army of the commonplace, let us write what we can, always of course doing our best, but not surprised or disappointed if we fall short of literary excellence; and let us congenially read the letters of our fellows. Those who are gifted writers will enter in and please us by the exercise of their talents, but we need not feel left outside until the editor rises to the full measure of his self, and says, Ladies, I desire this Household to change its character, and become a literary essay shop where only about half a dozen writers will find standing room.

Then we will rise in a body and depart; but if I understand aright such is not his desire or design; he gives us this page for our occupation, our entertainment and profit, if we can make it so; and means by so doing to confer the pleasure upon the largest possible number, viz. the majority.

We are a very young Household yet, but we are growing very fast, and presently the quality of our work will improve, though it will never be a literary feast. But we are not looking for that here. In our bookcases we can find plenty of fine literature. Here we want simplicity, good feeling, good taste, good sense, good fellowship, and congeniality, the bringing together of those who otherwise would never meet, and the wholesome discussion of everyday topics, and troubles where each can help little, and be helped in turn. Of course we are going to be commonplace, that is what life must be—but sometimes there will be many showers of wit and wisdom, many a shining thread of love and sympathy, and many wise words from those who have lived, loved, and suffered, and through that discipline have learned how to live noble and worthy lives. To those who suggest a higher order of writing let me say one word. Don't advise, go to work and do; set an example of what ought to be—as Yankee Sojourner would say—blaze a trail, and all who can follow will be quick enough to do it. Bring in your improved topics, don't say they ought to be brought in. Advising and criticising are about the easiest things done in the world. Reformers must lead the way, or they can have no following; so set a fashion for a higher style, and those who can will adopt it, and those who can't will go on as the Lord made them, and be counted herewith. It's no use for the majority to be ruled out.

CONSTITUTION - BY-LAWS


1. NAME. The name of this ASSOCIATION shall be the Preston County Growers' and Stock Breeders Association.


2. OBJECT. Its object shall be to encourage the growing of corn and the breeding of improved grades or kinds of stock; to encourage more intensive raising of all kinds of stock, and to improve the interests of the growers of Preston County.


3. OFFICERS. The officers of the Assoc. shall be President, Vice President for each district represented, and a Treasurer, Recording Secretary, and a Corresponding Secretary, who shall be elected by ballot for the term of one year, or until their SUCCESSORS are duly elected.


4. DUTIES OF THE OFFICERS. The Vice President shall constitute a Board of Directors, three of when shall form a quorum. The Recording and Corresponding Secretary may be one and the same person. The respective officers shall perform such other duties as may be requested from the nature of their offices.


The President and Recording Secretary shall prepare program of exercises for each regular meeting and publish the same in the papers of the county for four weeks preceding the meeting.


5. MEMBERSHIP. Any person may become a member at any time by paying $1 to the Treasurer or Recording Secretary, and have his name recorded.


6. MEETINGS. There shall be two meetings yearly, one on the first Monday of January and the other on the first Monday of October. The place may be fixed upon by the Association at the last preceding meeting. The President and Board of directors may call special meetings.


7. The Vice Presidents shall represent the County Association in their respective districts, and do all in their power to carry out and further its objects by district organizations and other means.


8. The Board of Directors shall see that the instructions of this Association are carried out, make all necessary arrangements at place selected by the Association for holding its regular meetings and audit account of Treasurer, take bond from him if necessary, and perform such other duties as the nature of the office may require.


9. The election of officers shall be held at the January meeting.


10. The Treasurer shall make an annual report at the January meeting.


11. No money shall be paid out of the treasury except by order of the Association, or upon the order of the President and Recording Secretary.


12. QUORUM. Five districts being represented, or one third of the officers being present, shall constitute quorum.


13. This Constitution may be changed by two thirds vote of all the members present, at any regular meeting. Notice of intention to change must be given at a previous meeting.


Jas. W. Brown, President.


Wm. G. Worley, Secretary.

WASHINGTON, Jan. 31.—A letter has been received at Department from Mr. Eckenstein, the United States Consul at Amsterdam relative to the coming International Exposition at that city. The consul says he has received no communication from any person in the United States asking any information whatever concerning the exposition. Up to the time of writing space to the about 440 square feet had been secured by or for six persons or firms in the United States. A considerable number of Americans have, however, made inquiries at the office of the Committee of the exhibition for all sorts of information. England, France, Germany, Belgium, Switzerland, Austria, Persia, Spain, Italy, China and Japan will participate in the exhibition. Commissioners have been appointed by the Governments of England, France, Belgium, Spain, China, Japan, and British and French colonies.

Applications for entire sections must be made before December 1, 1883. The unconcern and indifference manifested by American manufacturers in this regard causes surprise and disappointment in Amsterdam. The success of the exhibition the Consul declines to predict.

Mt. WASHINGTON, August 18th, 1883.


Messrs. Editors An article appeared in THE USIOS of July 25th, under the above caption which while it contained much valuable information on a very important subject, was still incorrect in some respects, and also omitted the names of several plants found in this region which are reputed to be poisonous.


Most people residing in the country are acquainted with the vine called poison oak and the swamp sumac, commonly known as poison ash but few are familiar as they should be with those plants which, while they may be handled without danger, are poisonous when eaten by man or beast. Ignorance in this respect might lead to fatal results and it would be well for all persons to avoid handling or placing in their mouths unknown species of plants, and none should attempt to gather herbs and roots for medicinal purposes who are not experts in the business.


The writer of the article above alluded to, while calling attention to the "cicuta water hemlock, common in our meadows and known as cowbane," fails to name a much far dangerous herb, the "mum" which grows on upland pastures. This has green and purple stem from 10 feet high, with flowers in umbels, like carrot, and exhales a fetid odor when bruised. It is declared to be "powerfully narcotic" it is used in medicine and it is pretty well known among country folks as poison hemlock. The common Parsnip, too, although wholesome and nutritious as a garden vegetable, when growing wild is pronounced by botanical writers to be acrid and poisonous.


Among the whortleberries there is one species reputed to be poisonous. It bears large green fruit. It is said the deer feed upon these, hence they are called in some localities "deer berries." There is another genus of plants closely allied to the whortleberries, and particularly abundant in the tide-water region of our State, which should be regarded with suspicion—the genus Andromeda. There are several species of this shrub bearing pretty looking blossoms, which tempt one to pluck them. One of them, called in the books the Maryland Andromeda, has a bad reputation and is injurious to cattle which eat it.


But by far the most dangerous class of plants found in our State are those of the Nightshade tribe, to which belong the Irish potato, eggplant, tomato, red pepper and tobacco, and the flowering plants Petunia, Nicandra and "tea berry." Prof. Wood, in his class book of Botany, says a large portion of the genera of this order are pervaded by narcotic principle rendering the berries and fruit dangerously poisonous, while at the same time several of the species afford wholesome and nutritious food, not because they are free from the narcotic principle, but because it is expelled in the process of cooking ripening, in the tubers of the potato and the fruit of the tomato and eggplant. One species of Nightshade is a common weed about farm buildings and on roadsides. Although the berries of all of them are said to be poisonous to the human family, it is asserted that wild animals and even hogs eat them with impunity.


The Jimsonweed—a "Jameson of crimson"—is abundant on vacant lots around the city and is often found about farm yards. The seeds of this weed, before they reach maturity, are said to possess horrid sweetness which has often tempted children to eat them with fatal results. The Lycium or "tea berry," a trailing shrub with orange berries, which may be found about many farm houses, is also of the Nightshade fam. lily. Its fruit is not considered poisonous but it would be well to avoid putting it in the mouth. Poke berries, though eaten by birds, are considered dangerous to human beings, but when matured in alcohol they have some reputation as a remedy for rheumatism. Speaking of poke berries, as A. Lincoln used to say, reminds me of a little story. Some years ago, in a town in Pennsylvania, when pie crust was very scarce, an old Frenchman furnished the citizens with admirable pies the contents of which he persistently refused to divulge. At last it leaked out that the Frenchman's pies were made of poke berries, and the secret spread among the housewives of the town one after another tried her hand at poke berry pie but all who ate of them were made sick. The result was that during the remainder of the season the Frenchman had no competition in the poke berry pie business, his method of preparing the fruit being a mystery which none of the townspeople could unravel.


Lobelia inflata is not poisonous, the learned and distinguished Dr. Gray and all other botanists who state the contrary, notwithstanding. The assertion by Dr. Gray that "less than a teaspoonful of the seeds or powdered leaves of this plant would destroy life in few hours" only proves that the utterances of the most learned are not always to be relied upon. The statement in Wood's Botany—and which has often appeared in print in agricultural papers—that Lobelia "causes salivation in horses in autumn" is no doubt equally unfounded. Several of the Lobelias, all of which are more or less nauseating, are used in medicine as emetics but they are no more poisonous than pecac, and they do not possess the narcotic properties attributed to them by some botanical and medical writers.


The mushrooms are another order of plants, some of which are poisonous, and frequently life is sacrificed through the ignorance of those who gather them. Some years ago I wrote an article for THE USIOS on the edible mushroom, and gave directions for selecting them so as to avoid the species having poisonous properties. As the season for them is at hand it might not be amiss to repeat what was before written, which, if the editors of THE USIOS permit, will do in another communication. A. W. SWISHEY.

And this may possibly happen. But, whether it does or not, it is certain that the latter aspirant has undertaken work the successful completion of which cannot fail to win for him an enviable position in the world of letters. Mr. Hubert Bancroft's researches in his chosen field bore their first fruit when his "Native Races of the Pacific States" made its appearance in five large volumes, several years ago. The work then begun is to be carried forward in the form indicated in the volume before us; and if the plan adopted be followed out it bids fair to be within the limits prescribed for it, more comprehensive in its scope and more elaborate in its details than any historical digest yet attempted in this country. The first three volumes of the series are to be devoted to Central America. From that point the author will cover Mexico and the North Mexican states, California, Nevada and Utah, Oregon, Washington, Idaho and Montana, and ending with British Columbia and Alaska.

This is a most stupendous undertaking, but Mr. Bancroft seems to be adequately equipped for it, as well in the material he has brought together as in the intelligence, industry and enthusiasm with which he prosecutes his work. wheel at all; thus if man buys ticket with

write to some one asking them to call out his
number and see it go in the wheel. These gen-
erals were brave soldiers and no doubt are hon-

not posted as to what constitutes an honest lot-
tery drawing, and their statement shows it.

Efforts for MR. Tilden.

Chicago Tribune, yesterday

Hon. Thomas A. Hendricks arrived yesterday from Indianapolis, and is stopping at the Grand Pacific, with Mrs. Hendricks. He is here to attend the taking of depositions in cases with which he is connected; The ex-senator is looking the picture of health, and seems to be in excellent spirits. His recent speech at Council Bluffs being mentioned in so far as it had reference, he had thought it best to take that occasion to express his idea on the subject. STEUBENVILLE, April 14.—More knowing individuals who have been predicting the ruin of the city of Steubenville in the event of James McConyille's elevation to the Mayoralty can now have time to reflect over their foolish assertions, and good many of them are having the manhood already to acknowledge their mistake in the man. Thos. Kinney is the First ward's guardian. Kinney has the reputation of being a man of pluck, and will no doubt make an efficient officer.


Isl. Merriman, a colored cop, was on Marion's force the first year of his administration, and was well liked. He will look after the safety of Second Ward citizens, and can boast of being the only "colored" policeman in this State.

One of the best appointments of the bunch was that of Philip Diguan, who will have charge of the Fifth Ward. The Fifth needs a good man, and they have one in the person of Diguan. He is a gentleman, and will do his duty.

the seed is up sprinkle ashes around the
plants, but not in direct contact with
them when very young. Gas tar, when
used for impregnating water, which
should be sprinkled over plants, is very
obnoxious to all kinds of insects, and
may be used freely on turnips, cabbages,
squashes, melons, and other vegetables,
as it is not injurious to plants.
No crop will give better returns for
thorough cultivation and stirring up of
the soil, although many farmers make
the mistake of leaving the turnip patch
to shift for itself after the plants are
once well started.


WHEN TO CUT TIMOTHY.


A writer in the Tribune says: My
rule for cutting Timothy, when it is
in its very best estate, if possible, and
that is when the major part of the field
is in bloom. Some of the seeds then are
in milk, and most of them, perhaps, are
not through, for I never cut my
grass, wet or dry, because I am ready, as
some do. But my rule is to begin the
first day after I think the gluten, starch
and sugar are most abundant in the
stalk and leaves, and hurry on the work
as fast as possible during the dry weather
and while there is plenty of hot sun
shine. I never cut grass for hay when
it is wet from much dew or even light
rain.


LOW-PRICED WOOL.


If there is any one lesson taught by
the history of wool-growing in the Uni
ted States, it is that the best results are
secured by the men cautiously pursuing
the business through all vicissitudes of
the market-place and keeping about
their flocks all the economies and com-
forts experience has shown to be neces-
sary to their locality or condition, neither
selling when others are discourag-
ed, nor buying when others are over
sanguine. Experience has repeatedly
shown that sheep of some kind, in ger-
tain numbers, can be made profitable on
a majority of farms. Exceptions can be


made for poor selections or faulty handling of flocks in re-
spect to the breed at the crossing to secure best results in wool and matter,
and the most serious disappointment
will be borne by those who have either
just gone into business, lured on by the
brilliant prospects of a year or two
since, and those whose land has become
too valuable to pursue sheep husbandry
as specially.


ONE of the most plainly discernible
things in business these days is that
live stock, grain, wool, and farm pro-
ducts throughout, are lower than they
were at any time in the year 1882. Av-
eraging these things, they are not below
the limit of profitable production, yet
as compared with those ruling a year
ago, many lines of values seem very low.
The country has been enjoying a boom,
in fact; and now that things are settling
to the point of average production and
compensation, the change seems greater
than it really is. Because our cattle and
hogs bring less money than we have
been realizing for some time is no rea-
son why we should overlook the fact
that both kinds of stock can still be
grown and resold with profit. To
sell stock at the ruling prices of 1882 is
an experience which one can strike but
once or twice in a lifetime; while the
country is now getting down toward the
basis of values on which the great bulk
of our agricultural wealth has been
amassed. In comparison with last year's
prices, stock is in comparison with
the prices of 1879 and 1880, high.
The outlook is full of hope and promise,
and 1883 bids fair to be one of the most
successful agricultural years in the his-
tory of the country.—Pittsburgh Stock
man.

Please let me know the exact age of a
horse, when the bride teeth appear. Do
these teeth appear in mares? 2. How
do you ascertain the age of a horse by
the mouth when he has reached fourteen
or fifteen years? —1. The tusks of the
bride teeth always appear in horses at
from four to four and half years.

earlier period than draught or heavy
breeds. Tusks appear in mares, but are
not so marked as in stallions or geld
ings, and in some mares are not present
at all. 2. In old horses the teeth are all
stripped of flesh or gum to great ex-
tent; the upper ones, when the mouth

stead of being flat, and extending later-
ally to meet each other. This is an ap-

years, the after treatment of the animal
will affect the appearance of his mouth,

correspondent of the Breeders Gazette
says: "The question is, where does the
farmer's principal business lie, on the
road in the buggy or carriage, or on the
farm on the road in the farm
wagon? I think the farm and wagon
is the proper place for his horse at least
if not for himself, if he wishes to make
his farm productive. If so, he wants a
horse that can turn good, deep furrow,
draw heavy load on the road; to be

he can possibly be trained to. This
combined with strong, closely-built bo-
dy and limbs, good style and steady
mild disposition, should, to my mind
constitute the principal points of the
farmer's horse."

We here propose to give short accounts of our trip to the meeting, the country through which we passed, the impressions made upon our minds, &c. Mr. Fort's Remarkable Stroll Across the
Delaware River.

Philadelphia Record

At 5 O'Clock Wednesday afternoon the Delaware river front between Chestnut and Walnut streets fairly swarmed with humanity. The cause of the unwonted excitement was the announcement in the morning papers that Mr. R. C. Fort, of this city, was to attempt to walk across the river to Kingsley Park. At half past 5 O'Clock the hero of the hour made his appearance on the scene, and was greeted with round after round of applause. He was an elderly man, tall and thin, and had sandy chin whiskers. His costume was a marvel of brilliancy. On his head he wore a rakish, broad-brimmed hat of gray felt, turned up at one side and fastened with a huge glass emerald and a nodding plume of scarlet feathers. His jacket, which was three sizes too small, was of crimson velvet, slashed with orange silk, and his trousers, which were of the Zouave pattern, were of crimson plush. White cotton hose dressed his well-turned limbs, and his shoes were such as ordinary mortals wear. Forcing his way through the crowd, Mr. Fort descended to the water and stepped into two small skiffs of peculiar pattern, which were to serve him as shoes in his watery walk. They were about six feet long, eighteen inches wide and apparently extended to that depth beneath the water, about six inches showing above. From the centre of each an upright handle reaching up about 6 feet afforded support, and they were utilized to work a pair of oars, one of which struck out behind each "shoe." On its "decks" were a supply of boat hooks and a small hatchet, the use of which did not appear. The start was made at 5.55 O'Clock and Mr. Fort struck out bravely for the island, but the sculling arrangement instantly refused to work, and, notwithstanding his frantic efforts to make headway, the venturesome voyager proceeded rapidly adrift up the river on the bosom of the tide, surrounded by the row-boats and showered with sarcastic comments from the small boys along the docks. For over an hour he battled valiantly with the treacherous waves, by which time he was at least half mile to the northward of the island. The tide then turned, and gradually carried him back again, and at 10 minutes before he went ashore on the north side of the Park, where he was instantly surrounded by an admiring crowd, and two burly young men carried him on their shoulders to the bar-room. He returned to the city in a row-boat.

Twice the Turks have been under its walls, in 1529 and, in 1683, the last time
their army consisting of 100000 men.
This time the Turks were routed and the
city relieved by the Duke of Lorraine
and the Pole, John Sobieski, and the
Turkish commander, Kara Mustapha,
was promptly bowstringed by the Sultan.
The ramparts erected by the Turks are
still visible in places. In 1619 the Be-
hemian Protestants under Count Thurn
besieged the city to compel the Emperor
Ferdinand to educate his children as
Protestants, the Count being in league
with the citizens with them who were
mostly of the Reformed faith. The Em-
peror, who was stanch Catholic, made
sturdy resistance, and was relieved by
assistance once more by the Poles.


Napoleon was in possession of Vienna
twice, in 1805, after the battle of Auster-
litz, and in 1809, after the battle of
Wagram. However, Napoleon was in
possession, one time or another, of
almost all the cities of Europe. So
Vienna had no reason for exception.


In 1849 the revolutionary movement
which began at Paris and spread over all
Europe extended to Vienna and for a
time it was in possession of the insur-
gents. Prince Metternich fled to Eng-
land. The Emperor left the city and
for a time it was probable that Austria
would become a Republic. But Prince
Windischgratz with the Bohemian army,
and Jellachich with the Croatians, came
down upon the insurgents and after
fierce struggle they were overpowered.
Robert Blum, the leader of the Red Re-
publicans was shot, with many others,
and the royal family were put in possess-
ion of the city once more.


Vienna is built in a most peculiar
manner. Following the plans of the old
Romans, a central point was established
and the city built around it, and then a
wall around the city. So Vienna proper
is a great spider web. The center is the
platz in front of St. Stephens Church,
from which streets and alleys radiate in
all directions till they reach what were
the walls which extended entirely
around the city. As the city grew in
size and population additions
were made outside the walls, at first in
their immediate neighborhood, and then
going further and further away until
now any one of the suburbs is much
larger than the old city itself.


There is the little stream from which
the city takes its name, the Wien, which
forms one division of the suburbs; that
empties into the Danube Canal, and there
begins another addition, and so on all
around the city. In the course of these
additions as they may be called, they
became so large that it was found neces-
sary to do away with the walls that
separated them from the city proper,
which was done in 1859, and the space
they occupied was leveled and laid out
in broad, well-paved streets that are
now the chief pride of the Viennese.
These streets, three miles in length,
make a circle, and are known as the
Ring. They entirely surround the
old city, and from them handsome
streets lead in all directions to all the
suburbs. R. Locke, in Toledo Blade.

He ducked his head to let the dust pass over, turned into the box Office entrance, and went immediately to his private Office. "Will you see a reporter of THE TRIBUNE?" said the reporter over the partition.

"Oh, is that you?" the impresario shouted back. "This interview in The TRIBUNE this morning with Nilsson is outrageous. Come in and I'll talk about it."

"Now, do you know," began the manager, after the reporter had helped himself to a seat. "I've been reading this article pointing to the interview printed in The TRIBUNE yesterday with Madame Nilsson, and by Jove—well, let me review it with you." Mr. Mapleson tipped back in his chair and reread the article, commenting on it as he read, something in this wise: "'Oh my dear Mapleson; he's no colonel. No colonel, eh? Oh, he isn't. She says further that she'd like to punch my head. Punching heads! It's simply ridiculous. Punch my head!'" and Mr. Mapleson unconsciously felt of his head to see if it had been punched already.

But I must read this again. She says if I'd see him, I'd feel like quoting Shakespeare to him, and say to him, 'Yes; that Go to expression she must have obtained from Ada Cavendish or Ella Wesner or some tragedienne equally conversant with the sayings of Shakespeare.' A Nantucket letter to the New York
Evening Post says: Five hundred ship
wrecks are recorded as having occurred
on the island since commerce began in
its waters, and this by no means includes
all. The first wreck was in 1864, when
an English ship went to pieces here, and
the passengers and crew were murdered
by the Indians. In the revolution sew
eral prizes made by our privateers came
ashore on the south side, and their rich
cargoes, strewn along the beach, were q
treasure-trove to the inhabitants whom
the war had impoverished. Some of the
saddest disasters have been recent. My
travelling companion detailed a few that
may serve as instances.


On the evening OF December "a, 1865,
tho schooner Haynes from San Domingo,
was discovered off the west end of the
island fast on shoal. A boa. from the
Humane society's station boarded her
and found the cabin warm and good
fire in the stove, but not a soul on
board. All had embarked in the boats,
and had been overwhelmed. The ro-
nance of this wreck lies in the fact that
her captain was a resident of the island,
and had been married just before sailing

OF successful plant growth. The late
John III. Klippart, an authority on
drainage. condensed the advantages Of
tile drainage under twelve heads: i.
"The drainage removes stagnant waters
from the surface No soil can pro
duce useful crops when it is covered or
its surface permanently saturated with
water. In wet seasons clay lands hold
| the rainfall in the lowest places, and
when it finally evaporates the crop is
! destroyed and the surface is baked and
hard. This evaporation also uses a
| great amount of heat, which would
| otherwise warm the soil. We see, there
| fore, that if the water that fails upon
| the soil remains until removed by eyap-
| Grafton, all the heat which should be
making the soil warm is being wasted
| IN evaporating the water. One expert
menter made a number of tests in two
| adjoining fields, one drained the other
undrained. The average temperature
of the soil in the field that had been
drained was six and one-half degrees
| higher than in the other. This is another
reason why drainage enables the earlier
cultivation of a field and lengthens the
season; the ground becomes warm so
much earlier in the spring and remains


warm later in the fall.


?. :. 1t removes surplus water from
under the surface.


/ The best condition of the soil for sue
cessful plant growth is found when
the particles of the soil are moist, but
when there is no standing water among
these particles. In wet seasons, if no
adequate means are provided forire-
moving the excess of moisture that falls
upon the soil. it will be continually sat-
urated, and the crops will be as surely
Grovaed out as though water appeared
on the surface Again, if the soil be
! full of water that which falls upon it
| in rain must flow off over the surface,
carrying with it much of the best and
finest of the soil. Water standing in
the soil causes the vegetable matter to
undergo acetic fermentation. thus ren-
dering the soil sour and unfit for cult
walton. The freezing out of winter
grain il oftener than from any other
cause produced by the formation Of ice
in the upper part of the soil, which
/ throws out the plant and leaves it to
perish. With good drainage. the soil
would b. dry when it was .timef for freez-
ing, and what is called 'heaving" would
not occur. 8. at lengthens the sea-
sons.n Often the yield of crop de-
| ponds greatly on the time it can be put


in the ground. A few days difference
in sowing may make mucn in yield.


The work can be better and more eco
nomically done because there is more
time to do it. If land is drained it can


be more thoroughly pulyerized, and


be in better condition for nourishing
the growing crops. Air in the soil IS
necessary as well as moisture. but it
can not penetrate the baked surface.


On drained land the plants will send
their roots deeper into the soil. When
a plant begins to grow in the spring in
an undrained soil the roots will not pen
citrate into the cold lower soil filled with
water, but run along through a. few
! inches of the drier surface. When the
dry weather comes the sun completely
dries this out and the plant, having no
other supply, stops growing. On land
that has been underdrained in the con-
dition described as most favorable for
plant growth, meist but with no stand
ing water between the particles, the
plant sends its roots far and deep.


The remainder of Mr.. Klippart' S
points condensed, most Of which we have
touched upon, are: It deepens the soil.
| 1t warns the soil. 1t equalizes the tenn
perature of the soil during the season Of
growth 1t carries down soluble sub
stances to the roots of plants. It pre-
vents heaving and freezing out. 1t
prevents injury from drought. 1t i'm
proves the quality and and quantity of
| the crop. 1t increases the effect of
manures. 1t prevents rust in wheat and
rot in potatoes. .a


One important question with all
who have land that needs drain
| ing is the cost. Not that it will
/ not pay but that it needs capital
| to do it. 1t can and has frequently
been demonstratedltha drainage pays
and pays well. In very wet seasons it
frequently happens that the total fall
ure or success of a crop depends entire
ly on the drainage. DR.. Townsend, Of
Ohio, states on this point: Sc one year
: underdrained part of a field at a cost
of $22.50 per acre, and at harvest it
/ yielded 20 bushels more per acre than
the undrained part of the field, and as
the crop brought $1.25 per bushel, the
extra yield paid all the expenses of
draining, and left me a little in
pocket Such instances can be found
all over the country. John Johnston,
of Geneva, N. Y, underdrained a
heavy clay farm that produced a good
crop of wheat only in the most favor
able seasons, and made it SO that he
grew for many years an average of 40
! Nushels per acre. ~a
| On many farms the principal ex-
pense will be for the tile alone, the
work being done by the ordinary help
of the farm at times when other work
is slack. The plans must be laid at the
outset so as to do no superfuous work.
| When the outlet is fixed and the line
established for the main drain, there is
the place to begin; and be sure to make
this drain large enough so as to answer
the purpose during heavy falls of rain
when it is most needed.


/ Many who have put in drains have
found during the late wet weather that

OF successful plant growth. The late
John H. Klippart, an authority on
drainage, condensed the advantages of
tile drainage under twelve heads: 1.
"The drainage removes stagnant waters
from the surface. No soil can pro-
duce useful crops when it is covered or
its surface permanently saturated with
water. In wet seasons clay lands hold
the rainfall in the lowest places, and
when it finally evaporates the crop is
destroyed and the surface is baked and
hard. This evaporation also uses a
great amount of heat, which would
otherwise warm the soil. We see, there-
fore, that if the water that falls upon
the soil remains until removed by evap-
oration, all the heat which should be
making the soil warm is being wasted
in evaporating the water. One expert
maker made a number of tests in two
adjoining fields, one drained the other
undrained. The average temperature
of the soil in the field that had been
drained was six and one-half degrees
higher than in the other. This is another
reason why drainage enables the earlier
cultivation of a field and lengthens the
season; the ground becomes warm so
much earlier in the spring and remains
warm later in the fall.

2. It removes surplus water from
under the surface.

3. The best condition of the soil for suc-
cessful plant growth is found when
the particles of the soil are moist, but
when there is no standing water among
these particles. In wet seasons, if no
adequate means are provided for re-
moving the excess of moisture that falls
upon the soil, it will be continually sat-
urated, and the crops will be as surely
destroyed as though water appeared
on the surface. Again, if the soil be
full of water that which falls upon it
in rain must flow off over the surface,
carrying with it much of the best and
finest of the soil. Water standing in
the soil causes the vegetable matter to
undergo acetic fermentation, thus ren-
dering the soil sour and unfit for cult-
ivation. The freezing out of winter
grain is oftener than from any other
cause produced by the formation of ice
in the upper part of the soil, which
throws out the plant and leaves it to
perish. With good drainage, the soil
would be dry when it was time for freez-
ing, and what is called "heaving" would
not occur. 8. It lengthens the sea-
sons. Often the yield of crop de-
pends greatly on the time it can be put
in the ground. A few days difference
in sowing may make much in yield.

The work can be better and more eco-
nomically done because there is more
time to do it. If land is drained it can
be more thoroughly pulverized, and
be in better condition for nourishing
the growing crops. Air in the soil is
necessary as well as moisture, but it
cannot penetrate the baked surface.

their roots deeper into the soil. When
a plant begins to grow in the spring in
an undrained soil the roots will not pen-
etrate into the cold lower soil filled with
water, but run along through a few
inches of the drier surface. When the
dry weather comes the sun completely
dries this out and the plant, having no
other supply, stops growing. On land
that has been underdrained in the con-
dition described as most favorable for
plant growth, moist but with no stand-
ing water between the particles, the
plant sends its roots far and deep.

points condensed, most of which we have
touched upon, are: It deepens the soil.

perature of the soil during the season of
growth. It carries down soluble sub-
stances to the roots of plants. It pre-
vents heaving and freezing out. It
prevents injury from drought. It im-
proves the quality and quantity of
the crop. It increases the effect of
manures. It prevents rust in wheat and
rot in potatoes.

who have land that needs drain-

not pay but that it needs capital

EDITOR INTELLIGENCER:—I see in to-day's
Register an article from Mr. Mulligan in re-
gard to the work done on Water street. He

The Emperor was greatly troubled, and

ruler of the country, but the Princess,

and ready to fire, she proclaimed who
she was, and by the style of her manner
and address she won over to her side not
only the soldiers but the commander
himself, and she and her retinue were


permitted to land. The shock was
too great for her father, the Emperor


who, looking from the deck of his


steamer, expected to see her shot down
like a dog, and in the day after he was


permitted to land and to proceed in his


native place, Petit Goaves, he suddenly
expired.
